volumes.title: Opening the Account
volumes.text:
I am Linus Orrery, bookkeeper to Pell and Daughter, corn-factors of Emberwick, and in thirty-one years I have never left a sum unrecorded. It struck me last week that my dreams go entirely unaccounted for. This ledger is to correct that. Each morning I shall enter what the night gave and what it took.

First entry. I dreamed of a shop built on the half-landing of a staircase. Its shelves held glass jars, and in each jar was an afternoon: a wet one, a golden one, one with a brass band in it. The shopkeeper was a tall grey heron in an apron. She did not offer to sell me anything. She handed me a bill, folded once. It read: One afternoon. Outstanding.

Debit: one afternoon, owed to persons unknown. Credit: nil. I do not recall incurring it, and I am not a man who forgets a debt.

volumes.title: An Audit by Pike
volumes.text:
Second entry in the dream ledger of Linus Orrery, bookkeeper. Having been billed for one afternoon by a heron in an earlier dream, I slept warily.

Last night my books were audited. The auditor was a pike, a large one, in half-moon spectacles, standing upright at my desk in the counting-house in two inches of clear water. He turned every page with a fin. He checked each column twice. I have never been so nervous and so flattered at once. At last he pronounced. The figures were correct to the farthing. The books were, however, short of weather. Thirty-one years, he said, and not one entry for wind.

Credit: a clean audit. Debit: a remark I cannot stop thinking about. I looked through the real ledgers this morning. He is right. There is no column for it.

volumes.title: The Sideways Stairs
volumes.text:
I keep this ledger of my dreams as I keep the accounts at Pell and Daughter: daily, and in ink. Last night I went looking for the shop on the staircase, where a heron once handed me a bill for one afternoon.

I found the stairs. They went sideways. I climbed along them for some time, holding the banister, which was warm, and came out not at the shop but in our own granary. Every sack on the floor had been untied. In each one, curled on the grain, lay a sleeping cat. There were cats to the rafters, tabby, black, marmalade, all breathing together like a slow sea. I sat down among them. Nobody asked me for anything.

Debit: none. Credit: warmth, one granary’s worth, entered here at an estimate since I had no means of weighing it.

volumes.title: A Loan of Feathers
volumes.text:
Dream ledger, fourth entry. Linus Orrery, bookkeeper, in sound health and good standing, except with a certain heron who says I owe an afternoon.

Last night I borrowed wings. The lender was a goose on the bank of the Ember, very businesslike. Her terms were one feather back per mile flown. I signed with a reed. Then I was up over the town, higher than the weathercock, with my coat-tails streaming and the river laid out below like a line ruled in silver. From there I saw it: a chimney where no house stands, halfway up the air above Stair Lane, smoking gently. The heron’s shop. I flew four miles looking for a door and found none.

Debit: four feathers, paid promptly on landing. Credit: one aerial view, and the knowledge that the shop keeps a fire in. Somebody expects me.

volumes.title: The Bill Itemised
volumes.text:
I am a bookkeeper, and I enter my dreams in this ledger each morning before the counting-house opens. Last night the shop on the staircase came back, with its jars of afternoons and its heron in an apron. I asked, politely, to see my account in full. She took a pencil from behind her head and wrote on the bill beneath the first line. It now reads: One afternoon, blue, with wind. Promised. Not delivered.

Promised, by me. The shop only holds the paper. I asked to whom it was promised. The heron looked at me for a long moment, the way Miss Pell does when I have asked something she thinks I could work out.

Debit: one afternoon, now with particulars. Credit: nil. Note: I have never broken a promise in business. I am less sure about before business.

volumes.title: The Moon Takes Sugar
volumes.text:
Sixth entry in the dream ledger. I, Linus Orrery, bookkeeper, received a caller in my sleep. The moon came to tea. She arrived by the window, which she had to take sideways, and sat in the good chair. She was smaller than expected and took three sugars. We talked of the price of barley, on which she was well informed, having looked down on a great many fields.

Then she asked, quite gently, about the afternoon I owe. Everybody up there knew, she said. It had been outstanding a long while. She only wondered if I had forgotten whom it was for. I said I had. She patted my hand with a cool one and said it would come to me, and that the kite would help.

Debit: three sugars. Credit: one hint. I own no kite. I entered the word anyway and underlined it.

volumes.title: Inventory of the Attic
volumes.text:
I record my dreams here as strictly as I record corn at Pell and Daughter. Last night’s needs two columns. I dreamed I was taking inventory in the attic of the house where I was a boy. One rocking horse, lame. One box of marbles. One kite, red, with a tail of knotted rags, hanging from a nail. When I touched it I woke, and I remembered.

I was fourteen. My sister Dora was nine. We built that kite together, and I promised her that on the first blue windy afternoon we would take it up Lantern Hill. That same week I was offered a stool in the counting-house. I started on the Monday. There has been no afternoon since.

Debit: one afternoon, blue, with wind, owed to my sister these thirty-one years. Credit: I know now what I owe. A bookkeeper can do nothing until he knows that.

volumes.title: Interest Accrued
volumes.text:
Linus Orrery, bookkeeper, eighth entry. I now know that the afternoon I owe was promised to my sister Dora, when we were children, for flying a red kite. Last night I went back to the shop on the staircase to ask what such a debt comes to after thirty-one years.

The heron took me behind the counter. There were shelves I had not seen, running back farther than the building could allow, and every jar on them was labelled in my own handwriting. My afternoons. All the ones I had not used, put by. Some had gone a little cloudy. She held one to the lamp and said they keep remarkably well. Then she named the interest. It was not more afternoons. It was only that I should enjoy the one I paid.

Debit: unchanged. Credit: stock in hand, far larger than supposed.

volumes.title: A Letter to Dora
volumes.text:
This ledger is for dreams, but today’s entry begins awake. I, Linus Orrery, wrote to my sister Dora, who lives at Saltby on the Grey Coast with her daughter Tilly. I told her I owed her an afternoon with a kite, thirty-one years overdue, and asked when I might pay it. It took four drafts. The first three read like invoices.

Then I slept, and dreamed of the post. My letter was carried by a hedgehog in a peaked cap. He bore it along the coast road in both front paws, very upright, and would not be hurried. At each milestone he stopped, checked the address, and went on. I walked beside him and did not mind the pace.

Debit: one stamp. Credit: a letter safely in the dream post, and, I hope, the real one. The hedgehog would accept no tip.

volumes.title: Leave of Absence
volumes.text:
Dream ledger, tenth entry, kept by Linus Orrery of Pell and Daughter. I am preparing to pay my sister Dora the afternoon of kite-flying I promised her as a boy. In last night’s dream I was mending the red kite. I had no paper, so I patched it with pages torn from the corn ledgers, and the columns of figures made a handsome pattern against the sky. I felt no alarm whatever at tearing them out. That is how I knew I was asleep.

This morning I bought brown paper, paste, and a ball of string. Then I knocked on Miss Pell’s door and asked for an afternoon off. She put down her pen. In thirty-one years, she said, I had never asked. She had begun to wonder if I was real.

Debit: ninepence for materials. Credit: one afternoon, authorised. It only wants wind.

volumes.title: Waiting on the Wind
volumes.text:
I, Linus Orrery, bookkeeper, have a kite built and an afternoon granted, and am waiting for the right weather to pay a very old debt to my sister. My dreams this week have been waiting too. On Monday I dreamed of a pond without a ripple. On Tuesday, a flag hanging straight down. Last night I climbed to the shop on the staircase to ask whether the afternoon could be sent round. The heron was dusting jars. They do not deliver, she said. I must collect in person, and bring my own wind.

By the morning post came Dora’s answer. She remembers the kite. She remembers the promise better than I did. She and her daughter Tilly will come on Thursday.

Debit: three nights of flat calm. Credit: a date. The weathercock on the corn exchange swung round to the west at noon. I watched it do so.

volumes.title: Paid in Full
volumes.text:
Final entry. On Thursday afternoon I, Linus Orrery, climbed Lantern Hill above Emberwick with my sister Dora and her daughter Tilly. The sky was blue. The wind came steady out of the west. The kite went up at the second attempt and stayed there two hours, and Dora laughed exactly as she did at nine. Tilly held the string. I did no sums of any kind.

That night I dreamed of the shop on the staircase. The heron took my bill, the one that read One afternoon, blue, with wind, and stamped it. Paid. Then she counted change into my hand. I had not expected change. It was one evening, in a small jar, to spend as I like.

Debit: nil. Credit: nil. The account is balanced and I am closing the ledger. There is a new book at the office, however. It has a column for wind.

volumes.title: January: Frost on the Step
volumes.text:
January. Moon full on the ninth, frost most nights. I am Mina Dray, seamstress, of Thimble Lane in Emberwick, and I walk in my sleep. I have decided to keep an almanac of it, since no one else publishes one.

This month I walked once. I woke at four in the morning on the step of Rudd’s bakery, barefoot, with my shawl on inside out. The baker was already up. He gave me a hot roll and his wife’s slippers and said the smell of bread has fetched in stranger things than me. A curious matter. Next morning there was a quilt square in my workbasket that I did not make, at least not awake. It shows a brown loaf, done in wool, in stitches finer than my best.

Advice to sleepwalkers for January: wear socks to bed. You do not know where you will want them.

volumes.title: February: The Watchman’s Bell
volumes.text:
February. Moon full on the seventh, wind from the fells, snow twice. This is the almanac of Mina Dray, seamstress and sleepwalker.

One walk this month. I woke standing at the door of Emberwick Library with my hand on the latch, at an hour when it is very properly shut. Beside me stood Mr Oswin Budge, the night watchman, holding his lantern low so as not to startle me. He said I had been waiting there ten minutes, quite patiently, like someone early for an appointment. He walked me home and has since hung a small brass bell on my gate. If it rings in the night he will know I am abroad and come along behind. In my workbasket next morning lay a second quilt square I do not remember sewing: a blue door, neatly hemmed.

Advice for February: befriend the watchman. He knows all the icy places.

volumes.title: March: Other People’s Washing
volumes.text:
March. Gales at the equinox, full moon on the ninth. I am Mina Dray. I sew by day and walk in my sleep by night, and this almanac keeps count.

One walk. The bell on my gate rang at two, and Mr Budge the watchman followed me to the drying green behind Tanner’s Row. He reports that I took down an entire line of washing, folded every piece, and stacked it in the basket with the pegs on top. Then I woke, holding a stranger’s nightshirt, and was mortified. Mrs Pettibone, whose washing it was, says it has never been folded so well and I am welcome any night. The third quilt square appeared in my workbasket: a white shirt on a green ground, with a tiny peg worked in brown.

Advice for March: if you must do housework asleep, do someone else’s. They are grateful.

volumes.title: April: An Umbrella for Two
volumes.text:
April. Showers daily, moon full on the seventh, cuckoo heard on the nineteenth. An almanac for sleepwalkers, kept by Mina Dray, seamstress, who is one.

One walk, a wet one. I woke on the bench under the church lychgate with my umbrella open. I was holding it rather to the left. The reason was a large tabby cat, sitting beside me perfectly dry, who looked up as if I had been slow to wake. Mr Budge the watchman was on my other side, wet through. He said the cat had the better half of the umbrella and he had not liked to ask. Quilt square the fourth, found in my basket and sewn by me asleep: a black umbrella with a striped tail showing beneath it. My sleeping self has a sense of humour I was not aware of.

Advice for April: carry a larger umbrella.

volumes.title: May: Under the Blossom
volumes.text:
May. Warm nights, moon full on the seventh, apple blossom at its height by the twelfth. I am Mina Dray, seamstress of Emberwick, and this is my almanac of walking asleep.

One walk, the pleasantest so far. I woke at first light in Hallam’s orchard, sitting against a tree, with petals in my hair and my lap. A blackbird was singing directly overhead. Mr Budge the watchman sat on the wall nearby, eating bread and cheese. He had followed the bell on my gate as usual. He said he could have woken me an hour sooner, but I was smiling, and in thirty years on the night watch he has learned to leave a smile alone. The fifth quilt square came next morning: a bough of pink blossom, every petal a separate stitch.

Advice for May: if you wake somewhere beautiful, do not hurry home.

volumes.title: June: Hardly Dark Enough
volumes.text:
June. Shortest night on the twenty-first, moon full on the fifth, no rain to speak of. From the almanac of Mina Dray, seamstress and sleepwalker, Thimble Lane.

There is scarcely enough night in June to walk in. I got no farther than my own back garden. The bell on the gate never rang, so Mr Budge the watchman knew nothing of it. I woke kneeling by the bean row with earth to my elbows. I had weeded the whole bed. Not a bean was disturbed, and every weed lay in a tidy heap on the path. I have never weeded so well awake. It is a little hard to be outdone by oneself. The quilt square I found afterwards, the sixth, shows a bean-vine climbing a pole.

Advice for June: leave the trowel where you can find it in the dark. You may as well be useful.

volumes.title: July: Counting on the Bridge
volumes.text:
July. Thunder on the third, moon full on the fifth, hay all in. I am Mina Dray, a seamstress who walks in her sleep, and I keep this almanac month by month.

One walk. I woke on the Ember bridge leaning on the parapet, with Mr Budge the watchman at my elbow as he always is when my gate bell rings. He said I had been counting aloud. Not hurriedly. One, a pause, two, like someone going over a list. I reached twelve, nodded as if satisfied, and woke. Twelve what? There is a seventh quilt square in my workbasket now, a grey bridge with a yellow lamp, sewn in the night like the other six. I laid all seven out on the table and looked at them for a long time.

Advice for July: when your sleeping self starts counting, pay attention. She may have a plan.

volumes.title: August: A Message on the Slate
volumes.text:
August. Moon full on the third, heavy dews, swallows gathering. The almanac of Mina Dray, sleepwalker, of Thimble Lane, Emberwick.

One walk, and I left evidence. The schoolhouse door is never locked. Mr Budge the watchman, who follows when the bell on my gate rings, says I went in, took the chalk, and wrote on the big slate in a careful hand. Then I dusted my fingers and let him lead me home. The schoolmaster found it in the morning and sent to ask if it was meant for him. It read: Four more. Nearly done. It was not meant for him. I have seven quilt squares that I sewed asleep, and an eighth came this month: a slate with a stub of chalk. Eight and four are twelve.

Advice for August: read whatever you write at night. It is the only post you will get from yourself.

volumes.title: September: Pinning Up the Map
volumes.text:
September. Fog in the mornings, moon full on the second, first fire lit on the twentieth. I am Mina Dray, seamstress and sleepwalker, and this month my almanac has more to report than a walk.

The walk first. I woke in the porch of the Brass Kettle, holding a lantern borrowed from its hook, with Mr Budge the watchman beside me in the fog. Ninth quilt square, by morning: a lantern in grey mist. Then I pinned all nine squares to the wall in the order they came. Bakery, library, drying green, lychgate, orchard, bean row, bridge, school, inn. They share one border and one thread. They are every place I have woken this year. I am sewing a map of my own walks, asleep, and it wants three more squares.

Advice for September: stand back from your work. You may find you have been making something.

volumes.title: October: The Needle Left Threaded
volumes.text:
October. Harvest moon on the first, leaves down by the twentieth, geese going over. I am Mina Dray, seamstress, and I have learned that I sew a quilt in my sleep, one square for each place I wake.

This month I tried to catch myself at it. I sat up in my chair with the lamp lit and strong tea. I remember the church clock striking one. Then it was morning. My slippers were full of leaves, and the tenth square lay finished in my lap: the churchyard yew. The needle had been left threaded. Mr Budge the watchman says I went no farther than the yew, and that my walks grow shorter. He also told me he retires at the year’s end. I did not like to ask who will follow the bell then.

Advice for October: you cannot stay up late enough to meet yourself.

volumes.title: November: As Far as the Gate
volumes.text:
November. First hard frost on the eighth, moon full on the twenty-ninth, dark by five. From the almanac of Mina Dray of Thimble Lane, who walks in her sleep and has sewn ten quilt squares that way since January.

One walk, the shortest of the year. Mr Budge the night watchman was passing at midnight. I came down my own path, reached the gate, and stopped. I did not open it. I put up my hand and rang the brass bell he hung there, once, like a visitor. Then I turned round and went back to bed. He says he raised his hat, though I could not have seen. Eleventh square, in the morning: a garden gate with a small gold bell. One remains. I have hemmed the others together and left a space.

Advice for November: it is no defeat to turn back at the gate.

volumes.title: December: The Quilt Entire
volumes.text:
December. Longest night on the twenty-first, snow lying, moon full on the twenty-ninth. I am Mina Dray, seamstress, and this closes my almanac of a year’s sleepwalking.

On the longest night I did not walk at all. I woke in my own bed at eight, having slept straight through, and the twelfth quilt square lay on the pillow. It shows a bed, with a small figure asleep in it under a patchwork of twelve colours. I sewed it into its place before breakfast. Mr Budge the watchman retired that week. I gave him a scarf I had knitted awake, which is why it is uneven. The quilt is on my bed. I sleep under the map of everywhere I went, and go nowhere.

Forecast for next year: sleep, mostly. The bell stays on the gate. I like the sound when friends call.

volumes.title: The Brass Plate
volumes.text:
I, Ignatius Plume, late of the umbrella trade, have this day fixed a brass plate to the door of 4 Candle Row, above the cheesemonger. It reads: I. Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions. Hours Ten to Four. I appointed myself. There was no one else to do it.

In this casebook, and nowhere else, I record a difficulty. To the best of my knowledge I have never had a dream. I go to bed, and then it is morning. I do not consider this a bar to practice. A doctor need not have measles.

Case the first. Mrs Orla Pym, of Tanner’s Row, dreamed that her teeth were piano keys and that a small man in a tailcoat was tuning them. Interpretation: she is to come into music. Fee: fourpence. She has since bought a concertina. Her neighbours have called on me, though not, I think, to offer thanks.

volumes.title: The Flying Baker
volumes.text:
From the casebook of Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions, 4 Candle Row, Emberwick. I interpret other people’s dreams, having none of my own to distract me.

Case the second. Tobias Rudd, baker, dreams three nights in seven that he is flying over the town seated in a bread tray. He is not frightened. He is hot. He passes the church weathercock at eye level and it turns to watch him go. Interpretation: flight signifies ambition, and a tray signifies trade. Mr Rudd will rise in his profession. I advised him to order a taller hat in readiness. Fee: one cottage loaf.

Addendum, a week later. Mrs Rudd has opened the bedroom window, which was painted shut, the room being directly over the ovens. The flying has stopped. I maintain that he rose, in a sense. He has kept the hat, and looks well in it.

volumes.title: A Goose Gives Advice
volumes.text:
I am Ignatius Plume, formerly umbrellas, now the only Interpreter of Night Visions in Emberwick. I keep this casebook faithfully, including the cases that go sideways.

Case the third. Abel Haddock, farmer in the Lowlands, dreamed that his grey goose walked into the kitchen, sat in his chair, and advised him in plain words to sell the bottom field. Interpretation: it is well known in my profession that geese in dreams mean the reverse of what they say. I told him on no account to sell. Fee: six eggs.

He kept the field. In the autumn it came up thick with mushrooms, which he sold at market for a good deal more than barley fetches. He credits me. The goose, he reports, will not look at him. I note for my own guidance that the principle concerning geese I made up on the spot. It appears to be sound.

volumes.title: Posy’s Blue Door
volumes.text:
Casebook of Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions, above the cheesemonger in Candle Row. A difficult client today, aged nine.

Case the fourth. Posy Marchbanks paid in advance with a pearl button and sat with her boots not reaching the floor. She says every dream she has ends the same way. Whatever it has been about, a picnic, a pony, her arithmetic, at the end there is a blue door. It is shut. She wakes before she can try it.

I had nothing. I said I must consult my books. She asked how many books I had. I have one, and it concerns the repair of umbrella ribs. She said she would come back. I have put her button in the cashbox, as I do not feel I have earned it. A private note. I, who have never had one dream, should rather like to see that door.

volumes.title: One Dream Between Two
volumes.text:
I am Ignatius Plume. I set up as Interpreter of Night Visions with a brass plate and no qualifications, and today I was required to act as a magistrate.

Case the fifth. The Dabb twins, Corwin and Clem, ferrymen on the river Ember, came in quarrelling. They have had the same dream on the same night. In it one of them rows a boat upstream through stars, while the other sits in the stern eating a pie. Each insists that he was the one with the pie. Interpretation: the dream is held in common, like the ferry. I ruled joint ownership. They are to take turns, one to row and one to eat, changing over at the new moon. Fee: a free crossing.

They left satisfied, which surprised all three of us. I do not dream, but I can tell when two people want the same pie.

volumes.title: Late to His Own Birthday
volumes.text:
From the casebook kept at 4 Candle Row by Ignatius Plume, self-appointed Interpreter of Night Visions and former mender of umbrellas.

Case the sixth. Mr Silas Tench, collector of the market tolls, dreams that it is his birthday. A party is laid in a marquee, with a cake and a band. He runs toward it across a field, but he has his toll-book under one arm and must stop at every gate to enter it. He arrives as the band is packing up. Somebody has kept him a slice. Interpretation: I said he needed a holiday. Fee: threepence.

I record that this was correct. He took a week at the Grey Coast and has not had the dream since. I had grown so used to being wrong in a helpful direction that being right has left me unsettled. I shall try not to make a habit of it.

volumes.title: On Not Dreaming
volumes.text:
This entry is not a case. I, Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions in Emberwick, have spent a week trying to obtain a dream of my own, having never yet had one.

Monday: a quarter-pound of the strongest cheese from the shop downstairs, eaten at bedtime. Result: thirst. Tuesday: slept with my head to the north. Result: a stiff neck. Wednesday: a sprig of marsh mint under the pillow. Result: a pleasant smell. Thursday I simply asked, aloud, politely. I slept nine hours and saw nothing whatever.

Posy Marchbanks, aged nine, called on Friday. She is the child whose dreams all end at a shut blue door. She reports a development: the door now has a knocker, brass, shaped like a closed umbrella. I did not tell her what trade I followed before this one. She looked at the stand in my hall for some time, however.

volumes.title: The Schoolmaster’s Stairs
volumes.text:
Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions, 4 Candle Row. I mended umbrellas for thirty years and have interpreted dreams for nearly one. I learn as I go. Case the eighth. Mr Ashby, the schoolmaster, dreams of climbing stairs. They have no top. He carries forty slates and may not put them down.

Interpretation, first attempt: stairs signify a wish to rise in the world. Mr Ashby replied that he lives in a cottage of one floor, likes it, and wishes to rise nowhere. Second attempt: then it is not the stairs that matter. It is that there is no banister. He wants something to hold on to. I advised him to ask the school board for an assistant. Fee: waived, as I had needed two tries.

He asked. They gave him one. He tells me the stairs now have a handrail, and a landing with a chair on it.

volumes.title: Night Visions of a Cat
volumes.text:
From the casebook of Ignatius Plume, Emberwick’s Interpreter of Night Visions. My practice widens. Case the ninth. Mrs Orla Pym brought in her cat, Admiral, in a basket. He twitches in his sleep. His paws run and his whiskers work. She wished to know what he sees, and whether he is happy.

The client would not describe his dream, so I was obliged to observe it. I sat by the basket for an hour with my notebook. I recorded eleven twitches of the left forepaw, four of the tail, one small noise like a creaking hinge, and a long sigh.

Interpretation: mice, in the past tense. He is remembering triumphs. I pronounced him a contented animal with a distinguished career behind him. Fee: none asked, though Mrs Pym left a saucer of cream. I have never had a dream myself, and I envied the cat a little.

volumes.title: Posy Knocks
volumes.text:
I am Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions, who has never had a dream. Posy Marchbanks, aged nine, came up my stairs today to report on hers, which have always ended at a shut blue door.

Last night she knocked. Nobody answered, so she tried the handle, and it opened. Behind it was a room. It was quite empty, she said, and clean, like a house before the furniture comes. There was one chair. In the chair an old man with white side-whiskers was sound asleep, with nothing going on around him at all. She did not like to wake him.

Her interpretation, offered free: the door was mine. It was shut because nobody was at home to dream. She had been knocking on it from her side for months. I have white side-whiskers. I gave her back her button. I could not speak for a moment.

volumes.title: The Interpreter Prepares
volumes.text:
Casebook of Ignatius Plume, 4 Candle Row. No clients today. I shut at noon to attend to a case of my own.

A child of nine, Posy Marchbanks, has dreamed her way through a blue door into an empty room and found me asleep in it. She believes it is the place where my dreams ought to be. I interpret night visions for a living and have never had one. I am inclined to take her opinion over mine.

Preparations, therefore. I have painted my own front door blue, two coats, so that I shall know it. I have oiled the hinges. I have put a second chair in my bedroom, in case of company, and a plate of ginger biscuits. I am going to bed at eight and leaving the door on the latch. If anyone should knock tonight, from either side, I mean to be in.

volumes.title: A First Vision
volumes.text:
I, Ignatius Plume, Interpreter of Night Visions, have had a dream. It is my first. I set it down this morning before it could get away. There was a knock. I opened a blue door, and Posy Marchbanks stood there holding a pearl button. I asked her in. The room was full of open umbrellas, every one I ever mended, hanging in the air, and it was raining upward from the floor. We had tea under a green one. That was all. It was splendid.

I took it straight to Posy at the school gate for interpretation, being too close to the case myself. She is nine and considered it gravely. It means, she said, that I was asleep, and that she had been right.

Fee: one button, which I paid. I have since altered my brass plate. It now reads: I. Plume. Night Visions Listened To.

volumes.title: To Wren, a Year On
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next January, this is you, a year ago, aged fifteen, writing on the first evening of the year. I began last month as apprentice to Mr Osric Vane, bookbinder, of Paste Lane in Emberwick. Mrs Larch at the library keeps a Tomorrow Drawer, where a letter may be left sealed for a twelvemonth. I mean to leave you one every month.

Some questions, so you know I was curious. Can you sew a straight line through a gathering yet? I cannot. Do your hands still smell of paste? Are you taller?

I shall also tell you my dreams, since nobody else wants them. Last night I opened a book and the pages were snow, real snow, quite untrodden. I was afraid to turn one in case I marked it. Be kind when you read this. I am doing my best. Yours, Wren.

volumes.title: About the Cat
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next February, it is me again, from a year back, in my second month at Mr Vane’s bindery. I must tell you about the cat. You know him, of course, but I want you to remember how it was at the start.

His name is Bodkin. He is grey, and enormous, and sits on top of the standing press all day with his paws folded, watching me work. When I make a mistake he closes his eyes. Mr Vane says Bodkin has seen eleven apprentices and approved of two.

Last night I dreamed he was as tall as the door. He wore spectacles and asked to inspect my indentures. He read every line, then sat on them. So here is my question. Has Bodkin ever once sat on your lap? I should only like to know it is possible. Yours, with gluey thumbs, Wren.

volumes.title: Crooked Stitches
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next March, I hope you are well and have forgotten today. I am fifteen and three months into my apprenticeship at the bindery on Paste Lane, and this morning I sewed a hymn book with every gathering askew. The spine looked like a staircase.

Mr Vane did not scold. He handed me the little knife and said, unpick it. It took all afternoon. He told me that everything he knows he learned from doing it wrong first, and that he was very learned by my age. My face is still hot. If you remember this, I hope you remember it more coolly than I feel it.

I dreamed afterwards that I was sewing the river Ember to its banks, so it would lie flat. My stitches were perfect. The river thanked me and said it had been meaning to have that done. Yours, Wren.

volumes.title: The Sea, Unseen
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next April, here is a thing I am ashamed of and will only tell you. I am fifteen, I live nine miles from the Grey Coast, and I have never seen the sea. Gran says there was always something else that wanted doing.

Today at the bindery I repaired a ship’s log. It was stained with salt, and the paper had a ripple that would not press out. Mr Vane says paper remembers water. So this letter is a promise as well as a question. By the time you open it, you will have gone. Tell me I am right.

Last night the sea came to me instead. It walked up Paste Lane, quite low and polite, and waited outside our door. It did not come in. It only wanted to know when I was coming, and I said soon. Yours, landlocked, Wren.

volumes.title: Gran’s Plum Tree
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next May, this letter is about Gran’s plum tree, because you may need reminding how it stood this year. I am your old self, fifteen, apprentice bookbinder, writing at the kitchen table.

The tree is as old as I am. Gran planted it the week I was born, and it has never borne one plum. Every spring Gran says it is waiting for a reason. This morning it is white with blossom from top to bottom, for the first time, and she keeps walking out to look. I do not know what reason it has found. Perhaps you do.

I dreamed of the plums last night, already ripe. I bit one. Where the stone should be there was a tiny book, sewn properly, with pages the size of a thumbnail. The print was too small to read, and I woke. Yours, Wren.

volumes.title: A Blank Book
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next June, I have news, and you know how it ended, which I do not. Six months into my apprenticeship, Mr Vane the bookbinder has set me my proving piece. By the year’s end I am to bind one book entirely by myself: fold, sew, round, back, cover and finish. If it holds, I stay on.

It is to be a blank book. Nothing in it at all. I asked him what a blank book is for. He said that was the purchaser’s business, and went back to his glue pot. It troubles me, to spend six months making something with nothing in it. Do you know what it is for? You must, by now.

Last night I dreamed of a book that read me. It turned me over, quite gently, and seemed interested, though it skipped some parts. Yours, Wren.

volumes.title: Gold Leaf and Breath
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next July, you will laugh at this by the time it reaches you. I am fifteen and learning gold tooling at Mr Vane’s bindery, and this week I sneezed.

Gold leaf is thinner than anything. You lift it on a brush you have stroked against your cheek, and you must not breathe. I had a whole leaf laid ready over the spine of a prayer book. I felt the sneeze coming from a long way off. The gold went up like a startled bird and came down in small pieces on the cat.

Mr Vane laughed. I had never heard it before. It sounds like a drawer opening. Bodkin wore a gilded ear until Thursday and was unbearable. I dreamed of gold moths afterwards, hundreds, settling on my hands and staying exactly where I put them. Yours, sneezing, Wren.

volumes.title: I Went
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next August, one question you need not answer. I went. I am fifteen, I had never seen the sea, and on Sunday Gran and I rode the carrier’s cart nine miles to the Grey Coast, with sandwiches.

I am writing it down for you tonight in case a year rubs it smooth. It was much bigger than I had allowed for. It was loud. It kept arriving, over and over, and nobody on the beach seemed to think this remarkable. Gran took off her boots, which I have never seen her do out of doors. I brought back a flat grey stone. It is on the bench at the bindery, holding down endpapers. I hope it still is.

I dreamed last night that I bound the tide in quarter leather. It would not stay shut. I woke up pleased about that. Yours, salted, Wren.

volumes.title: Bodkin’s Verdict
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next September, three pieces of news from your younger self, the apprentice at the bindery on Paste Lane. First, Gran’s plum tree bore fruit. Seven plums. We ate one each on Sunday and gave five away, since she says a first harvest should travel. Second, I sewed all twelve gatherings of my proving piece, the blank book, and every one lies straight. Mr Vane ran his thumb down the spine and said nothing, which from him is praise.

Third. I left the sewn book on the bench and went for the paste. When I came back, Bodkin the cat had climbed down from the press and was sitting on it. Squarely, with his paws tucked. Mr Vane says that is the verdict, and there is no appeal.

I dreamed of nothing I remember. I think I was too content. Yours, approved, Wren.

volumes.title: What Frightens Me Now
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next October, in my second letter I told you I was afraid of the bindery cat. I am nearly sixteen, and I wish to correct the record: I am now afraid of something else.

My blank book, the proving piece for my apprenticeship, is almost done. It is rounded and backed and in its boards, and I chose green cloth with a brown leather spine. Soon there will be nothing left to do to it. That is the trouble. While I am making it, it might be good. Once it is finished, it will only be what it is. Is it like this every time? Tell me it wears off.

Last night I dreamed of a long shelf in the library, quite empty, with my name on a small card. I thought it would feel lonely. It felt like a room kept ready. Yours, Wren.

volumes.title: It’ll Hold
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of next December, I owe you a letter for November and you shall not get it. I was finishing my proving piece and had no words to spare. I am your self of a year ago, apprentice bookbinder, and tonight the blank book is done.

Mr Vane took it to the window. He examined it through his glass for a quarter of an hour. He held it by one board and shook it. Then he set it down and said, it’ll hold. I am to stay on. Bodkin the cat yawned, which I take as applause.

I still do not know what a blank book is for. Mine sits on the shelf, green and brown, with nothing in it. I dreamed last night that tomorrow knocked at the door, and I knew the knock. This is my last letter. The next move is yours. Wren.

volumes.title: Tomorrow Writes Back
volumes.text:
Dear Wren of last January, it is me. I am sixteen, it is the first evening of the year, and Mrs Larch has just handed me your first letter from the Tomorrow Drawer at the library. You asked me to be kind. You were doing better than you knew.

Your answers. Yes, I sew straight, mostly. I am taller by an inch. I have seen the sea twice, and Gran made plum jam. Bodkin, the bindery cat, is on my lap as I write, which makes the penmanship difficult.

As for the blank book I bound, I have found what it is for. I have pasted your letter onto its first page. I shall open one each month and add it, and when the eleventh is in, this reply goes last. I dreamed nothing last night. I slept, and when I woke it was tomorrow. Yours, as promised, Wren.
